Q: Can one use SetWindowLongPtr + GWLP_USERDATA to store data (not pointer) A:

I don't think there's any guarantee that it will never ever try to dereference it when not NULL.

I don't know why it would, but maybe some check because of some past attack on Word 97. It says that it is a pointer, so I guess it should actually be a pointer.

The problem with breaking little unspoken rules is that if you do it all the time, you will eventually run into an issue. And likely not initially but with some later OS / library update.

Don't always follow best practices.

But also don't habitually store random stuff in a value that is actually named a pointer ^^

Unless officially supported, of course.

You can get away with it with a fixed target, like this code is only for this version of the mars rover, which is guaranteed to run on this version of linux with this libc, and I've thoroughly tested that it works, and we really, really need to get rid of that indirection because we need that extra clock cycle.

But that's an unlikely edge case ^^

Q: Update start/stop time of state table and insert if state changes A:

Use stored procedure;

CREATE PROCEDURE insert_new_data ( -- adjust parameters datatypes according your table structure
    in_Device_id INT,
    in_State VARCHAR(16)
    )
BEGIN
    IF ( SELECT state
         FROM test
         WHERE Device_id = in_Device_id
         ORDER BY Starttime DESC LIMIT 1 -- maybe you'd sort by Stoptime
         ) = in_State 
    THEN
        UPDATE test
        SET Stoptime = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
        WHERE Device_id = in_Device_id
          AND state = in_State
        ORDER BY Starttime DESC LIMIT 1;
    ELSE
        INSERT INTO test VALUES
            (in_Device_id, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, in_State);
    END IF;
END

Q: Is it better to "pull" data inside a Node.js Worker Thread or "push" data from the main thread? A:

In most cases, the push-based model is the better practice.

worker_threads are mainly designed to offload CPU-intensive work from the main event loop. If workers also handle data fetching (DB/queue/network), they become responsible for both I/O orchestration and computation, which mixes concerns and makes the system harder to manage.

With the push model, the main thread:

  • pulls data from queues/DB

  • manages worker availability

  • distributes jobs to workers

Each worker only:

  • receives data

  • performs CPU-heavy processing

  • returns the result

This separation has several advantages:

1. Better separation of responsibilities

The main thread handles coordination, workers handle processing.
That makes the architecture easier to reason about.

2. Easier worker pool management

With push-based scheduling, the main thread knows:

  • which workers are idle

  • how many tasks are queued

  • when to scale workers up/down

With self-pulling workers, scheduling logic gets fragmented across threads.

3. Better queue/database control

If every worker fetches independently, you may get:

  • DB connection contention

  • uneven workload distribution

  • race conditions when claiming jobs

A centralized dispatcher avoids that.

4. Lower resource overhead

Workers are relatively expensive.
Using them only for CPU-heavy tasks avoids unnecessary I/O overhead inside each worker.

The pull model can still work if each worker owns an isolated data source or partition, but for general queue/DB processing, push-based orchestration is the recommended approach.

So:

  • Main thread = fetch + schedule

  • Worker thread = CPU processing

That is usually the cleanest Node.js worker architecture.

Q: Invalid or unsupported command "update" A:

The problem

You need to reconfigure your PATH so that the new command is found before the old one.

You can confirm that this is the issue by running:

echo $PATH

If that's the issue, you'll see something like ([...] referring to other content):

[...]~/Library/Android/sdk/tools/android:[...]:/usr/local/bin/[...]

Quick fix

Adding something like this to your ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc should fix it, but this is a bit of a hack (see below for a better fix).

You can also run this in your terminal to fix it for that session.

export PATH="/usr/local/bin/:$PATH"

Better fix

Find out what is adding these to the PATH in the wrong order. There are several ways that paths can be added to the PATH, such as (non-exhaustive list) ~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, .zprofile, .profile, .bash_profile, /etc/paths (note: not a script), etc.

Whatever is adding it should add the SDK tools to the end of the PATH, not the start

export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/Library/Android/sdk/tools/android"

Q: Managing requirements in IPython Notebook? A:

For notebooks specifically, static tools like pipreqs won't help much — imports are scattered across cells and often conditional. A runtime approach works better.

I wrote envcore which also has great notebook support:

envcore notebook analysis.ipynb

Or inside IPython/Jupyter:

python

%load_ext envcore
%envcore start
import numpy, pandas
%envcore snapshot

It traces what actually imports during execution and writes a manifest. envcore restore rebuilds the exact environment anywhere.
